newsitem.title: CHINA: HK Tel IDD deal rumours puzzle analysts.
newsitem.headline: HK Tel IDD deal rumours puzzle analysts.

text.p: Suggestions that Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd may get cash or land for giving up its stranglehold on international direct dial (IDD) calls in the territory drew a mixed response from analysts on Friday.
The monopoly is due to end in 2006, but Hongkong Telecom and its regulator, the Office of the Telecommunications Authority (OFTA), are discussing ending it before that date.
Rumours that a deal had been struck drove Hongkong Telecom shares up HK$1.30, or almost seven percent, to HK$20.40 at one point on Friday, before closing at HK$20.15.

"I haven't heard that today, though I've heard it about 1,000 times before," Morgan Stanley telecommunciations analyst Jeff Camp said, commenting on speculation Hongkong Telecom might be allowed to cash in on its land bank in Hong Kong's pricey property market.
"The question has always been: how valuable exactly is that land bank?" Camp added.
Analysts were sceptical of the suggestion that the government might agree to pay off Hongkong Telecom.
"It just doesn't seem like the government's going to put out a huge amount of cash to end the monopoly," said an analyst with a European brokerage.

Rather than paying the company hard cash to give up its monopoly, the government could reduce or eliminate the levy that Hong Kong Telecom would have to pay if it wanted to develop the land it leases from the government.

Such a move might also help the new Special Administrative Region (SAR) government in its goal of increasing the supply of housing if Hongkong Telecom opted to develop the land in that way, analysts said.
"It does kind of kill two birds with one stone. It's more palatable," the European analyst said.
BZW Asia analyst Lloyd Fischer said a deal based on the land bank would be solve the problem of compensation from the government's point of view.
"If the rumour was true, it would benefit the company and the public. I believe it would be more politically acceptable than paying a lump sum," Fischer said.
He said new technology meant that Hongkong Telecom needed fewer switching centres around the territory and therefore could have land to spare.
However, Morgan Stanley's Camp said he had estimated that losing the monopoly in 2000 would cost Hongkong Telecom US$3 billion in sheer value terms.
"That's a big chunk of money for the land bank to fill," Camp said.
OFTA director-general Tony Wong was not available for comment on the rumours.
A spokesman at Hongkong Telecom said, "We have no comment to make because talks are continuing."
